hood_landmark.Vieux Nice: Cours Saleya's flower market amid baroque lanes
hood_landmark.Cimiez: Musée Matisse and the Roman arena in the Cimiez gardens
hood_landmark.Liberation: Marché de la Libération's sprawling open-air food market
hood_landmark.Quartier des Musiciens: Ornate Belle Époque facades along Boulevard Victor Hugo

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing on the Promenade des Anglais, Old Town and around the station; caution near the station at night

hood_desc: Vieux Nice is the atmospheric old town, a maze of narrow baroque lanes packed with the Cours Saleya market, cafes and lively nightlife. It suits first-time visitors, foodies and those who want to be in the buzzing historic heart.

Cimiez is an elegant, leafy hilltop district of Belle Epoque villas, Roman ruins and the Matisse Museum. It suits culture lovers and travelers seeking a quiet, upscale residential base away from the crowds.

Le Port centers on the colorful Port Lympia marina lined with yachts, antique shops and trendy seafood restaurants. It suits visitors wanting an authentic, less touristy neighborhood with local character.
Liberation is a genuine local quarter built around its vibrant daily food market and close to the main train station. It suits budget-minded travelers and market-goers who want everyday Nicois life.

Quartier des Musiciens is a central grid of streets named after composers, steps from the beach, shops and the Promenade. It suits those wanting a convenient, walkable base that still feels residential.

water.note: Tap water is safe and well regulated across France.

transit.pay: Use the rechargeable Ticket Azur card or the Lignes d'Azur phone app; single tickets and cards can also be bought from tram and bus vending machines (coins or bank card) or from the bus driver. A single ticket costs about €1.50 (~$1.75) and covers transfers for 74 minutes, while a 1-day pass is about €5 (~$5.80).
transit.hours: Trams run daily from roughly 4:30am until about 1:30am, and buses on a similar span with most last departures around midnight; there is no all-night network, so very late trips rely on taxis.

transit.m: Tram Line 2 to Port Lympia, 30 min

food.name: Socca
food.desc: Giant chickpea-flour pancake baked blistering in a wood oven, scraped onto paper and eaten hot with black pepper. Nice's essential street food.

places.name: Chez Pipo
places.note: Serving socca since 1923 from a wood-fired oven; widely rated the city's best.

places.name: Chez Rene Socca
places.note: Order at one counter, drink at the next, eat standing on the street with locals.

places.name: Lou Pilha Leva
places.note: Communal benches and a fast turnover of socca, pissaladiere and fried snacks.

food.name: Salade nicoise
food.desc: The real thing: raw seasonal vegetables, olives, anchovy or tuna and hard-boiled egg dressed in olive oil - no potato and no green beans.

places.name: La Merenda
places.note: Tiny cash-only room run by a former Michelin chef; book in person, no phone.

places.name: Chez Palmyre
places.note: Bargain fixed-price menu of Nicois home cooking; reserve well ahead.

places.name: Le Safari
places.note: Long-standing terrace on the flower market, reliable for the classic version.

food.name: Pissaladiere
food.desc: Bread-dough tart smothered in onions cooked to jam, finished with anchovies and small black olives. Sold by the slice all over the old town.

places.name: Chez Theresa
places.note: Market stall from a family that has baked socca and pissaladiere for generations.

places.name: Boulangerie Espuno
places.note: Award-winning bakery whose slices sell out by mid-afternoon.

places.name: Lou Pilha Leva
places.note: Handy for tasting pissaladiere alongside socca and stuffed vegetables in one stop.

food.name: Pan bagnat
food.desc: Round bread soaked in olive oil and packed with the salade nicoise ingredients, pressed until the juices run. Beach lunch in one hand.

places.name: Boulangerie Espuno
places.note: Properly soaked bread and generous filling; grab one on the way to the pebbles.

places.name: Cours Saleya market
places.note: Morning market stalls make them to order beside the flower and produce trestles.

places.name: Chez Rene Socca
places.note: Cheap and fast, part of the same street-food strip as the socca counters.

food.name: Petits farcis nicois
food.desc: Courgettes, tomatoes, peppers and onions hollowed out, stuffed with herbed meat and breadcrumbs, then baked until the tops go crisp.

places.name: La Merenda
places.note: Benchmark Nicois kitchen; the farcis change with whatever the market has.

places.name: Acchiardo
places.note: Family-run since 1927 on Rue Droite, a genuine old-town neighbourhood restaurant.

places.name: Chez Palmyre
places.note: Home-style cooking at prices that have barely moved in years.

food.name: Daube nicoise and raviolis
food.desc: Beef braised slowly in red wine with orange peel; the leftovers are chopped into the filling for Nice's own small ravioli.

places.name: Acchiardo
places.note: Old-school daube served in a dining room that has changed little in decades.

places.name: La Merenda
places.note: Handful of tables, no cards, no phone - but among the best Nicois cooking anywhere.

places.name: Le Bistrot d'Antoine
places.note: Popular modern bistro with a daily blackboard of Provencal braises; book ahead.

food.name: Bellet and Provence rose
food.desc: Nice has its own tiny AOC, Bellet, grown on the hills above the city, alongside the pale dry roses of the wider Provence coast.

places.name: La Part des Anges
places.note: Wine shop and bar focused on natural and small-grower bottles, including Bellet.

places.name: Cave de la Tour
places.note: Morning-to-night locals' bar where wine is poured by the glass at old-town prices.

places.name: Le Bistrot d'Antoine
places.note: Short, well-chosen regional list matched to the bistro cooking.

food.name: Pastis
food.desc: The southern aniseed aperitif, poured over ice and clouded with cold water. Ordered at any hour on a terrace before dinner.

places.name: Le Grand Cafe de Turin
places.note: Shellfish bar open since 1908; pastis and oysters under the arcades.

places.name: Les Distilleries Ideales
places.note: Busy corner bar with a long apero list and pavement tables in the old town.

places.name: Cave de la Tour
places.note: Unvarnished neighbourhood bar, the least touristy pastis in Vieux Nice.

landmarks: Promenade des Anglais
The palm-lined seafront boulevard along the Baie des Anges, iconic for its blue chairs and turquoise Mediterranean views.
Castle Hill (Colline du Château)
A hilltop park on the site of a former citadel offering the best panoramic photo of Nice's Old Town and coastline.
Vieux Nice (Old Town)
A maze of pastel-colored baroque buildings, narrow lanes, and markets that defines Nice's photogenic historic core.
Place Masséna
Nice's grand central square, known for its red ochre facades, checkerboard pavement, and Jaume Plensa statue installations.
Nice Cathedral (Sainte-Réparate)
A striking baroque cathedral with a tiled dome at the heart of the Old Town, a favorite architectural photo subject.
Russian Orthodox Cathedral, Nice
An ornate onion-domed Russian cathedral, the largest of its kind outside Russia, offering a striking exotic contrast to French Riviera architecture.
Musée Matisse
A red 17th-century villa housing the world's largest Matisse collection, set in the leafy Cimiez olive groves.
Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild
A Belle Époque mansion on Cap Ferrat near Nice, famed for its themed gardens and sweeping sea views.
Hôtel Negresco
A landmark Belle Époque palace hotel with a distinctive pink dome, an emblem of Riviera glamour on the Promenade des Anglais.
Opéra de Nice
An elegant 19th-century opera house in the Old Town with an ornate facade, a hidden architectural gem for photographers.

train.note: The only direct cross-border train is the coastal TER from Nice-Ville to Ventimiglia just over the Italian border, which runs roughly hourly and takes about 50 minutes. For Genoa, Milan or beyond, change at Ventimiglia onto a Trenitalia service and allow about 45 minutes to connect, as the two railways sell separate tickets. Nice-Ville is a 15-minute walk north of the seafront; TGVs reach Paris in about 6 hours and Marseille in 2h30m, and the Paris-Nice Intercites de Nuit sleeper runs overnight. The scenic Chemins de Fer de Provence narrow-gauge line to Digne leaves from a separate station, Nice CP, and is not covered by SNCF tickets.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the stops beside Nice-Ville station and at Nice Airport rather than a central bus terminal, and there is no staffed ticket office, so book online. Genoa is about 4 hours, Milan around 6 and Turin 5. Regional Zou! buses (https://zou.maregionsud.fr/) cover the whole Cote d'Azur for a low flat fare paid on board, including the run to Menton at the Italian border. Carry your passport for services crossing into Italy, where checks are made from time to time.

intl.to: Bastia, Ajaccio, Ile-Rousse & Calvi, Corsica (France) - from the Port de Commerce east of the old town
Porto Torres, Sardinia (Italy) - from the Port de Commerce

ferry.note: Ferries leave from the Port de Commerce (Terminal 1) about 20 minutes' walk east of the old town, reached by tram line 2 and local buses. Fast ships to Corsica take around 3-4 hours and run most days in summer but drop to a handful a week in winter. The Sardinia sailing to Porto Torres is summer-only, so check dates before relying on it. Vehicles and cabins must be booked well ahead for July and August, when Corsican crossings sell out.

half.name: Monaco
half.blurb: A glamorous principality with the Monte Carlo casino, superyacht harbor and clifftop palace.

half.name: Eze
half.blurb: A medieval hilltop village perched above the sea with tumbling stone lanes and coastal views.

half.name: Villefranche-sur-Mer
half.blurb: A peaceful seaside village with a sandy bay, colorful old town and sheltered harbor.

half.name: Cannes
half.blurb: The glamorous film-festival city offers the palm-lined Croisette and long sandy beaches.

half.name: Antibes
half.blurb: A charming walled town with a bustling market, old harbor and slower Riviera pace.

half.name: Menton
half.blurb: A sunny town near the Italian border known for lemons, pastel houses and gardens.
